text: So you have no excuse, whoever you are, when you sit in judgment on someone else. For in judging another you condemn yourself, since you, the judge, do the very same things.
And we know that God's judgment on those who do such things is according to the truth.
Do you really think, you who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape God's judgment?
Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, forbearance, and patience, not realizing that God's kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?
But by your stubbornness and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself for the day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment will be revealed.

versions.text: But by your hard and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath, when God's righteous judgment will be revealed.
versions.explanation: The Greek has two distinct terms, the noun σκληρότης ("hardness, stubbornness") and "unrepentant heart"; collapsing them into one adjectival phrase loses content. Also "storing up ... on the day" reads as though the storing happens on that day; "for the day" makes the future reference clear.

text: He will repay each one according to his works:
eternal life to those who by patient endurance in doing good seek glory and honor and immortality;
but wrath and fury for those who are self-seeking, who refuse to obey the truth and instead obey unrighteousness.
There will be affliction and distress for every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek,
but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
For God shows no partiality.
All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.
For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law.
They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness, and their conflicting thoughts either accuse or defend them
on the day when God judges the secrets of human hearts through Christ Jesus, according to my gospel.
But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God,
if you know his will and can determine what really matters because you are instructed from the law,
and if you are convinced that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of the immature, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you then who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal?
You who forbid adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?

versions.text: You who say that no one should commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
versions.explanation: "You who say that no one should commit adultery" is wordy and clumsy for oral reading, and it weakens the parallel with the preceding clause in verse 21 ("You who preach against stealing"). A tighter rendering preserves the rhetorical punch of the Greek participial construction.

text: You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?
For, as it is written, "The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you."
Circumcision has value if you keep the law, but if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
So if an uncircumcised man keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?
The one who is physically uncircumcised and yet fulfills the law will judge you who, for all your written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.

versions.text: The one who is physically uncircumcised and yet fulfills the law will condemn you who, for all your written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.
versions.explanation: The Greek verb here is κρινεῖ ("will judge"), not κατακρινεῖ ("will condemn"). Paul uses the stronger compound elsewhere (e.g., 2:1), so the distinction should be kept; "judge" is also more natural in the argument's rhetoric of comparison.

text: For no one is a Jew who is merely one outwardly, nor is circumcision merely outward and physical.
Rather, a Jew is one inwardly, and circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not the letter. Such a person's praise comes not from other people but from God.
